channel.title: FactTrench
channel.description: Amazing facts from the deep, and beyond — one true story every day.

item.title: The Deepest Fish on Earth Can Never Come to the Surface
item.description: Filmed 8,336 meters below the surface, the snailfish thrives under pressure that would crush a submarine — but a trip to the surface would destroy it.

item.title: This Jellyfish Can Live Forever — By Turning Back Into a Baby
item.description: When the immortal jellyfish gets old or injured, it does something no other known animal can: it restarts its entire life cycle from the beginning.

item.title: The Dumbo Octopus: The Cutest Animal in the Ocean's Darkest Place
item.description: With fins that flap like cartoon ears, the Dumbo octopus lives deeper than any other octopus on Earth — where there is no light, no ink, and no second chances.

item.title: The Deep-Sea Anglerfish: Her Boyfriend Becomes Part of Her Body
item.description: In the pitch-black deep sea, a male anglerfish bites his mate — and never lets go. He fuses into her body, sharing her blood, for the rest of his life.

item.title: The Fish With a See-Through Head: Meet the Barreleye Fish
item.description: The barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma) has a completely transparent head — and its bright green eyes rotate inside it. How this deep-sea fish sees through its own skull, why its 'eyes' are not its eyes, and how deep it lives.

item.title: Goblin Shark: The Pink 'Living Fossil' With a Slingshot Jaw
item.description: The goblin shark is a pink deep-sea shark from a family 125 million years old — and its jaws shoot forward like a slingshot, the fastest of any shark alive. Size, depth, the famous jaw strike, and why it is pink.

item.title: How Deep Is the Mariana Trench? Deeper Than Mount Everest Is Tall
item.description: The Mariana Trench reaches 10,935 metres (35,876 feet) at the Challenger Deep — deep enough to swallow Mount Everest with room to spare. The depth in feet and miles, the crushing pressure, and the few people who have been to the bottom.
